text_extraction: Given that the measurement of creative role expectations, cre- ative self-expectations, perceived necessity of performance improvement, and creative cognitive style was provided by one single informant (i.e., employees), common method var- iance (CMV) may exist and potentially bias observed relation- ships among study variables (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003). To test for CMV and its potential biasing effects, we conducted confirmatory factor analyses (CFAs) using the unmeasured latent method factor approach (Williams & McGonagle, 2016). Following the recommended comprehensive analysis strategy, we first evaluated the mea- surement model to check the convergent and discriminant validity of our main study variables. The results showed that our intended six-factor structure achieved quite good fit with the data (χ2[174] = 276.90, CFI = 0.98, TLI = 0.97, RMSEA = 0.04, SRMR = 0.04) and provided a significantly better fit than a series of alternative models in which the indi- cators of two or more variables were combined (p < 0.001 for all tests). We then added an orthogonal latent method variable to the basic measurement model to test for presence and equal- ity of method effects. The unmeasured latent method factor accounted for an average of 4.98% of the variance in the substantive indicators. Although we found evidence of a very small amount of CMV unequally distributed across substan- tive indicators, it did not affect key factor correlations that are associated with the core part of the research model and its proposed relationships. These findings indicate that CMV should have little to no effects on our hypotheses testing.

text_extraction: To address potential concerns of common method variance, we conducted several post- hoc tests. Utilizing Harman’s one-factor test with all self-report data, we found that one factor did not explain the majority of the variance in this study. As a more robust test and in line with past research (Conger, Kanungo, & Menon, 2000), we also created unmeasured latent method factors in structural equation modeling, connecting all self-report study items to this latent factor and constraining all the paths from this latent factor to be equal. By squaring the resulting regression coefficients from this latent factor, we observed that only 2% of the variance across these items was due to an unmeasured common factor. Furthermore, the association between the study variables was still highly significant (p < .001) when the unmeasured latent method factor was included in the model. Thus, it appears unlikely that our findings are explained by common method variance.

text_extraction: The unmeasured latent method construct technique (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, & Podsakoff, [61]; Williams & McGonagle, [89]) was used to control for the potential effect of methodological biases (such as the consistency motive and acquiescence). Hence, an unmeasured latent method factor was added to the measurement model, and all the observed variables were allowed to load on their respective theoretical constructs and on the method factor. The method‐factor loadings were constrained to be equal, for identification purposes. The fit of the model with the method factor was not significantly better than the fit of the original measurement model (Δχ 2 [5 df] = 10.046; p > 0.05). The observed variables also loaded on their corresponding latent factors. Finally, as Fuller, Simmering, Atinc, Atinc, and Babin ([24]) state, common method variance can exist at relatively high levels (70% or more) in typical survey‐based business research before common method bias is likely to alter the conclusions. Common method bias is thus unlikely to threaten the validity of the findings.

text_extraction: Because Harman's single factor test has been criticized by some for being an inferior, “insensitive test” (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003, p. 889), we decided to implement a second, more advanced approach to test for potential common method bias that evaluates the effects of an unmeasured latent method con- struct (ULMC; Podsakoff et al., 2003; Williams & McGonagle, 2016). Specifically, we compared the results of two models using structural equation modeling in Mplus Version 8. Model 1 included all theorized latent variables identi- fied by their respective self-reported items. Model 2 was identical to Model 1 with the sole addition of an uncorre- lated latent variable, which we named “CMV,” that was identified by all study items. We compared Model 1 and Model 2 and found that the factor loadings of the items on their respective constructs in Model 1 were all signifi- cant (p < .01), and the significance of the items on their respective constructs remained entirely unchanged by the addition of the CMV latent variable in Model 2. The average change in standardized factor loadings of items on the respective constructs between Model 1 and Model 2 was minimal (average Δβ = .20). Furthermore, the variance explained by CMV in Model 2, calculated as the average squared standardized item factor loadings, was 28%, which again falls below the 50% threshold. Thus, our results indicate there is insufficient evidence to assert a single latent factor (CMV) significantly modified the relationships among the study variables.

text_extraction: We need to address common method bias (CMB) as our study was based on self- reported data obtained from the same source (Podsakoff et al. 2003). In this study we focus on perceived performance and not on objective performance, which is common in the field of third sector organizations and in the general literature on network performance (e.g. Klijn, Edelenbos, and Steijn 2010; Liu, Takeda, and Ko 2014), making self-reports a relevant measurement method (cf. Conway and Lance 2010). Moreover, assessing objective performance in large N research is difficult or even impossible to achieve. In addition, other data sources that measure performance of CBIs (such as archival data) are unavailable, which makes the use of the survey as single method plausible (cf. George and Pandey 2017). Next, for most variables (including performance) we used multiple items in our measurement, and the scale reliability of all relevant constructs are well above general thresholds. Both reduce the likelihood of CMB (cf. George and Pandey 2017). We used ex-ante procedural remedies for reducing the likelihood of CMB in the survey design and ex-post statistical controls for testing CMB. Procedurally, we reduced the risk of CMB by allowing the respondents’ answers to be anonymous (Podsakoff et al. 2003, 888) and we separated between measures in the survey. In addition, we carefully constructed the items, by pretesting the survey among researchers and practitioners. This helps in reducing item ambiguity (Podsakoff et al. 2003). Statistically, we conducted the Harman one-factor test in SPSS and the unmea- sured latent method construct in AMOS to assess whether the majority of the variance could be explained by a single factor (Podsakoff et al. 2003). Results confirmed that CMB is not a major concern in this study.

text_extraction: To test for common method variance (CMV), we used a CFA-based version of Harman’s single-factor test (see, e.g., Malhotra et al., 2006). In AMOS, we specified a single method factor, such that it might cause all 14 indicators. The items loaded significantly on the single factor, suggesting that CMV might be source of variance in the observed items. That is, all 14 variables loaded on their theoretical constructs but also on the single latent common method factor (Podsakoff et al., 2003). Therefore, we added a separate marker variable, determined ex post to have no signi- fication correlation with the other items, to the measurement model (Lindell and Whitney, 2001). Next, we per- formed an unmeasured latent method construct analysis (Richardson et al., 2009; Williams et al., 1989) to check for the presence of trait and method factors. We observed both trait and method variance; however, a chi-square dif- ference test conducted on the trait-only and trait/methods (with methods held equal) models was invariant (Δχ2 = 0.00, p = 1.00). The equal loadings model also indicated that the common method bias would be equivalent to about 0.004, which is acceptable. Common method effects (and effects of missing variables) also may be mani- fest in the correlation of the error terms of the dependent variables in the structural model, but our analysis suggests minimal such bias.

text_extraction: The existence of bias due to common method variance (CMV) in mediation study designs can be a fatal flaw, as they are causal in nature. This study has a cross-sectional design, and the data were collected through self-report question- naires, thus increasing the risk that common method variance (CMV) may be present. To prevent these biases, we origi- nally used proactive measures and then ex-post statistical techniques (Podsakoff et al. 2003) to gauge the extent to which our results would be affected by CMV (see also, Conway and Lance 2010). In the proactive case, our sur- veyors guaranteed respondents’ confidentiality and anon- ymity in order to reduce social desirability bias. In addition, the researchers separated the items on perceived ethical leadership from those on employees’ self-reported peer-fo- cused OCBs, and these two scales’ items appeared on dif- ferent pages of the questionnaire. This yielded an effect of psychological separation in the respondents (Podsakoff et al. 2003). In the ex-post statistical technique, the possibility of common method bias due to CMV was tested using Har- man’s one-factor test (Podsakoff and Organ 1986). As such, we used exploratory factor analysis (EFA) for item reduc- tion, but fixing only one factor to extract and with no rotation. The principal component factor analysis conducted on the items of ethical leadership and peer-focused OCBs, and the factors of compassionate feeling, yielded one unique factor that explains 27.928% of the variance (rule of thumb estab- lishes that only a factor explaining more than 50% suggests significant CMV). In addition, we tested Harman’s one- factor test (Podsakoff and Organ 1986) by using SEM. By conducting unmeasured latent method construct, we con- trolled for the effects of a specified unmeasured latent CMV factor where all the manifest indicators loaded. All the regression weights were constrained to be equal. A com- parison of this restricted CFA factor model (v2 = 1304.937, df = 339, p\.001; GFI = .834, CFI = .834; IFI = .836; TLI = .815; NFI = .790; RMSEA = .067) with the unre- stricted CFA model calculated earlier (v2 = 1307.366, p\.001, df = 340, GFI = .769, CFI = .834, IFI = .835, TLI = .816, NFI = .790, RMSEA = .098) indicates that the change in fit statistics (Dv2d ð1Þ = 2.429, p [ .1) was nonsignificant. As the two models did not differ significantly, there is no evidence that CMV causes significant bias. However, each of the regression weights was .23, which squared is .529, that is, a tolerable 5% of common variance as an approximate estimate. All of these patterns suggest that common variance due to CMV undoubtedly exists, but it was not a major problem for the data (Podsakoff et al. 2003).

text_extraction: Political skill and IM were reported using a cross-sectional research design, and as such common method variance (CMV) needed to be statistically examined. We utilized the unmeasured latent method construct (ULMC) technique (Podsakoff et al. 2003; Richardson et al. 2009), which allows for partitioning of variance into three components: trait, method, and random error. According to Richardson et al. (2009), the ULMC procedure necessitates estimating four models. The first model, trait-only, tests the study’s measurement model consisting of 16 indicators pointing to positive IM latent variable (i.e., representing self-promo- tion, ingratiation, and exemplification factors), 18 indica- tors pointing to a political skill latent variable (i.e., representing social astuteness, apparent sincerity, net- working ability, and interpersonal influence factors), and a null method factor. The second model, method-only model, allowed estimation of the paths from the method construct to all the manifest indicators in the model while trait constructs were null. The third model, trait/method, involved estimation of paths from both trait and method constructs (i.e., method latent variable) to the manifest indicators and correlation among the trait constructs (i.e., IM latent variable was correlated with political skill latent variable). The fourth model, trait/method-R, was identical to the trait/method model, but covariances among the trait factors were constrained to the unstandardized values obtained from the trait-only mode. By constraining the covariance between trait factors, we are able to identify the level of variance explained solely from CMV when we compare the trait/method-R model to the trait/method model. Non-significantly different models suggest that CMV does not contribute to a significant portion of the variance in the latent variables. The trait-only (two-factor) model fitted the data signif- icantly better than did the method-only (single factor) model [v2 (404,405) = 929.4, p \ 0.01]. Further- difference more, there was no statistical difference between the fit of trait/method model and the trait/method-R model [vdiffer- ence2(374 375) = 0.06, ns]. Richardson et al. (2009) have asserted that bias due to CMV is present when the trait/ method-R model fits the data significantly worse than the trait/method model, whereas our results indicate no bias. Taken together, results from this analysis provide evidence that CMV is unlikely to confound the interpretations of our findings.

text_extraction: Several limitations of our studies should be mentioned. In study 2, EI and PSE were measured using self-report questionnaires. As with all self-report measures, common method variance and social desirability biases are a concern. We addressed these concerns in a number of ways. First, we used Harman’s one-factor test to deal with the potential threat of common method bias. The one-factor model accounted for only 27 percent of the variance, which is much lower than the acceptable cutoff of 50 percent. Second, we used the stricter unmeasured latent method construct (Williams, Cote, and Buckley 1989), whereby a CFA is conducted in which each item is loaded on its theoretical construct as well as on a latent common method factor (Podsakoff et al. 2003). As suggested by Richardson, Simmering, and Sturman (2009), as the model with both method and substantive components did not produce better fit indices than an identical model except with construct correlations constrained to the values obtained in the substantive-only model, common method bias is unlikely to be a problem in this study. Finally, we used an EI measurement that has previously demonstrated convergent and discriminant validity in research using multiple raters to assess EI (Law, Wong, and Song 2004).

text_extraction: In order to assess the extent to which inter-correlations among the variables might be an artifact of "common method variance" (CMV), we employed three tests (as suggested by Podsakoff et al., 2003. See also Lindell & Whitney, 2001): (a) the Harman’s single-factor method (a con- firmatory factor analysis, CFA, in which all items are simultaneously loaded on one single factor), (b) a common-latent factor (CLF), also known as Unmeasured Latent Method Construct (ULMC; Richardson et al., 2009), method (a CFA in which all items loaded on both – their expected factors and one common-latent factor are loaded on each of the items respectively, but are uncorrelated to their respective latent factors), and (c) a standard CFA to test the original construct. In addition, we examine the model fit and extracted explained variance (R2). The analyses were done by utilizing AMOS (v. 23) software with the function of Multiple-Group Analyses (as there are 12 different samples/groups). The results are presented in Table C1. The methods explained before produced explained variance (R2) as follows (Harman’s single-factor "outside" the parenthesis, and CLF method inside the parenthesis): Israel1 = 25.44% (23.15%); Israel2 = 28.01% (25.49%); Romania1 = 35.94% (32.71%); Romania2 = 29.88% (27.19%); Japan = 22.78% (20.73%); USA = 27.35% (24.89%); Pakistan = 30.07% (27.36%); Italy = 24.81% (22.58%); Turkey = 28.45% (25.89%); Brazil = 29.77% (27.05%); Germany = 34.64% (31.51%). This indicated that the CLF method produced less CMV. As can be seen in Table B1, the fits of the models vary. The worse fit, as expected, is derived by using Harman’s Single-Factor test. Then the standard CFA when the total construct (a unified one-factor) of HWI is tested instead of its dimensions. Next, the CLF method produced adequate fit indices, which highlight its importance over Harman’s Single-Factor test. While these results (in conjunction with the R2 extracted) do not rule out completely the possibility of same-source bias (i.e., CMV), following Podsakoff et al. (2003), the extracted explained variances are less than 50% (R2 < .50) indicating that CMV is an unlikely explanation of our investigation’s findings. Finally, the standard CFA with the two HWI dimen- sions (HWI-TC and HWI-WI) produced the best model fit (close to the "absolute" sense, apart from the c2-test; see, Byrne, 2010; Tabachnick & Fidell, 2013; Vehkalahti & Everitt, 2019). These results have led us to: (1) use the dimensions of HWI in further analyses, as they fit the data more than the total construct does and are more statistically (and theoretically) sane to use separately from one another, (2) create CMV-corrected/ adjusted dimensions of HWI (see, Lindell & Whitney, 2001; Podsakoff et al., 2003; Richardson et al., 2009) to account for any CMV that might confound the data.

text_extraction: We also assessed the presence of common method bia- ses, as though the experimental component of our study included conditions and manipulations, the non-experi- mental component included data (i.e., cultural orientation, perceived positive consequences of relational favoritism) collected from the same source (Chang et al. 2010). Our analyses reflect the two dominant approaches to assessing common method biases: (1) the unmeasured latent method construct approach and (2) the correlational marker approach (Richardson et al. 2009). First, we performed a series of Harman’s single-factor tests. As described in Podsakoff and Organ (1986), common method bias is a concern only if (1) one factor emerges in an exploratory factor analysis or (2) one factor in an exploratory factor analysis captures the majority of the covariance among measures. A series of factor analyses revealed that multiple factors accounted for significant variance in Brazil, China, and the U.S. Second, we explored the within-country and pooled correlation coefficients between the variables in the study. The correlations for many variables were small and non-significant. The minimal shared variance between many of the variables further suggests that common method bias is not a concern, as it is the shared variance that is representative of common method bias (Lindell and Whitney 2001; Richardson et al. 2009).

text_extraction: Although we collected data at two different times, all the variables were self-reported, and thus could be influenced by CMV (Podsakoff et al. 2003). Therefore, we tested whether CMV was present in our data using two techniques: the CFA marker technique and the unmeasured latent method construct technique. For the CFA marker technique, we employed prevention focus as a marker variable because it is theoretically unrelated to at least one of the focal variables (i.e., Mach)—furthermore, we found no significant correla- tion between prevention focus and any of the seven study variables (see Table 1)—and was measured with the same response scale used to assess other study variables (Richard- son et al. 2009). Following the procedure recommended by Williams et al. (2010), we estimated the baseline (which sets factor loadings from the marker variable to the indicators of seven substantive variables to zero), Method-C (which allows for loadings from the marker variable to the substan- tive indicators but forces them to be equal), and Method-U (which allows for loadings from the marker variable to the substantive indicators and does not force them to be equal, allowing them to be freely estimated) models. We tested for the presence of CMV by comparing the models. First, we compared the baseline model [χ2(df = 1068) = 1600.79; CFI=0.91; RMSEA=0.05] and the Method-C model [χ2(df = 1067) = 1597.96; CFI = 0.91; RMSEA = 0.05] to test the null hypothesis that the method factor loadings (assumed to be equal) associated with the marker variable are not related to each of the substantive indicators. The result of a χ2 difference test was insignificant [Δχ2(1) = 2.83, n.s.], thus providing support for accepting the null hypothesis (i.e., accepting the baseline model that assumes no method fac- tor loadings). Second, we compared the baseline model and the Method-U model [χ2(df = 1025) = 1548.29; CFI = 0.91; RMSEA = 0.05]. We also found an insignificant χ2 difference [Δχ2(43) = 52.5, n.s.], which indicated support for the null hypothesis that the baseline model fits the data better than the Method-U model. All these results that provided support for accepting the baseline model indicated that CMV was not present in the data. To confirm these results, we conducted an additional analysis using the unmeasured latent method construct tech- nique. Following the procedure recommended by Williams et al. (1989), we conducted another CFA in which we added a method construct to the measurement model, and allowed all measured indicators of the seven study constructs to load on the method construct as well as on their focal construct. The results indicated that adding the method construct improved model fit, but the proportion of variance accounted for by the method construct was only 5.75%, much less than typically found in other studies (25%; Williams et al. 1989). Therefore, based on all these findings, it is reasonable to conclude that CMV was not a serious problem in our data.

text_extraction: The existence of bias due to common method variance (CMV) can be a fatal flaw for mediation in mono- method/source studies because they are causal in nature. In this study, managers self-reported ethical leadership, employees self-reported their own alienation, and the measure of firm performance stemmed from managers’ subjective measurements of financial performance. The design of this study includes different sources and, in particular, the work alienation indicators, which have different sources from the variables in the basic relationship, thus mitigating the possibility of CMV (Podsakoff et al., 2003, 2012). Nevertheless, further proactive measures to prevent CMV were conducted. First, our surveyors guaranteed respondents’ confidentiality and anonymity in order to diminish the social desirability bias. In addition, the researchers separated the perceived ethical leadership items from those of employees’ self-reported firm performance, and these two scales’ items appeared on different pages of the questionnaire for managers. This practice yielded an effect of psychological separation in the respondents (Podsakoff et al., 2003). To examine the CMV problem (see also, Conway and Lance, 2010), Harman’s one-factor test was used (Podsakoff and Organ, 1986). First, we used exploratory factor analysis (EFA) for item reduction, but fixing only one factor to extract and with no rotation. The principle component factor analysis conducted on the items of ethical leadership and firm performance and the factors of feelings of alienation yielded a unique factor that explains 38.457% of the variance. Although 38.457% is an important amount of variance explained by a single factor, the rule of thumb establishes that more than 50% suggests significant CMV. In addition, we performed Harman’s one-factor test (Podsakoff and Organ, 1986) by using SEM. Through the unmeasured latent method construct, we controlled the effects of a specified unmeasured latent CMV factor on which all the manifest indicators load. All the regression weights were constrained to be equal. Each of the regression weights was 0.30, which squared is 0.09, that is, a tolerable 9% of the common variance as a rough guess. Moreover, the fit for this restricted CFA factor model (χ2 = 1,283.861, df=683,p<0.001;GFI=0.606,CFI=0.797,IFI= 0.800, TLI = 0.783, NFI = 0.651, RMSEA = 0.094) was worse than the fit of the CFA model with a latent method factor (χ2 = 1,511.864, p < 0.001, df = 807, GFI = 0.631, CFI = 0.830; IFI = 0.832; TLI = 0.815; NFI = 0.695; RMSEA = 0.092) because the chi-square difference test was significant (Δχd2(124) = 228.003, p < 0.001). All of these patterns suggest that CMV exists, but it was not a major problem for the data.

text_extraction: Because measurement errors can have a serious con- founding influence on empirical results, yielding mislead- ing conclusions, we then ran some additional models to assess the potential effect of common method bias. In doing so, we employed unmeasured latent method con- struct (ULMC) technique (William et al. 1989; Podsakoff et al. 2003). Following the procedure described by Richardson et al. (2009), we first estimated the trait-only model, a model identical to the basic model presented in Fig. 1, with inclusion of a null common method variance (CMV) construct. We then assessed both noncongeneric and congeneric trait/method model in which the paths from the CMV construct to all the construct indicators were added and estimated. Finally, we estimated the trait/ method-R model, a model identical to the trait/method model except that all the independent-dependent construct correlations were constrained to the values obtained from the trait-only model. The congeneric trait/method model in which the path coefficients were freely estimated fit the data better than the noncongeneric model in which the path coefficients were set equal (Dv2 = 61.372, d.f. = 15, p\0.01). Thus, we subsequently compared the fit of the trait/method-R model with that of the congeneric model. According to Richardson et al. (2009), if the trait/method model-R fits significantly worse than the trait/method model, there is sufficient evidence indicating the presence of common method bias. The trait/method-R model fit the data reasonably well with a v2 = 178.992 and d.f. = 88, (v2/d.f. = 2.034), AGFI = 0.946, CFI = 0.988, and RMSEA = 0.041. The fit of the congeneric trait/method model was also acceptable with v2 = 168.313, and d.f. = 82, (v2/d.f. = 2.053), AGFI = 0.945, CFI = 0.988, and RMSEA = 0.041. The v2 difference between the two models was 10.679, which is not significant with six degrees of freedom (p = 0.10). Because the two models fit the data equally well (i.e., no difference), our result pro- vided sufficient evidence that common method variance is not responsible for the results to be reported next (i.e., it has no potentially serious effects on research findings).

text_extraction: Common method biases are considered as one of the main sources of measurement error that threats the validity of the conclusions about the relationships between measures (Bagozzi & Yi, 1991; Nunnally, 1978; Podsakoff et al., 2003; Spector, 1987). To rule out possible common method biases, we examined common method variance at the measurement level using the unmeasured latent method construct technique (Williams et al., 1989). Specifically, following Podsakoff et al.’s (2003) suggestion and Richardson et al.’s (2009) procedure, we estimated four additional models. We first estimated the trait-only model, a model of a given independent–dependent construct pair, with a null method construct (χ2 = 704.566 with d.f. = 314 or χ2/d.f. of 2.244, GFI = 0.887; AGFI = 0.864; CFI = 0.926; TLI = 0.917; RMSEA = 0.054; SRMR = 0.046). Second, we estimated the trait/method (congeneric and non-congeneric) models by adding paths from the method construct to the indicators of all the independent and dependent constructs (congeneric: χ2/d.f. = 1.815, GFI = 0.917; AGFI = 0.891; CFI = 0.956; TLI = 0.946; RMSEA = 0.043; SRMR = 0.036; non-congeneric: χ2/d.f. = 2.215, GFI = 0.888; AGFI = 0.865; CFI = 0.928; TLI = 0.919; RMSEA = 0.053; SRMR = 0.045). Finally, the trait/method-R model was estimated by constraining independent–dependent construct correlations to the value obtained from the trait-only (first) model (χ2/d.f. = 1.798, GFI = 0.928; AGFI = 0.901; CFI = 0.977; TLI = 0.948; RMSEA = 0.042; SRMR = 0.036). According to Richardson et al. (2009), common method bias exists if the trait/method-R model fits significantly worse than the trait/method model. The results reveal that the chi-square difference between congeneric and non-congeneric trait/method models is significant (χ2 = 172.356, d.f. = 26, p < .05), indicating that the congeneric common method variance model fits better than the non-congeneric common method variance model. Furthermore, the chi-square difference between the trait/method-R model and the congeneric trait/method model is 15.539, which is not significant with 10 degrees of freedom (p = .11), indicating that the trait/method-R model fits the data equally well as the congeneric common method variance model. Taken together, the results provide sufficient evidence that common method variance is not responsible for the results reported as follows.

text_extraction: Given that our study used self‐report measures, which may lead to common method bias, we assessed the signif- icance of the common method variable in two different ways. First, we ran Harman's one‐factor statistical test (Podsakoff & Organ, 1986) and found that a single factor accounted for only 19.09% of the total variance. Then we used a single unmeasured latent method construct approach as our second post hoc statistical detection technique for common method bias. All items were loaded onto both their theoretical latent constructs and the unmeasured latent method factor (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003). All factor loadings of the items on their theo- retical construct remained significant, even after the effect of the common method factor was taken into account. Results showed that although the common method factor did improve the model fit, it accounted for 19.49% of the total variance, which is less than 25% below the criterion suggested by Williams, Cote, and Buckley (1989). The results of these tests indicate that common method bias is not a likely explanation for the relationship found in the current study.

text_extraction: All constructs examined in our study were measured through self- reported assessment tools. Therefore, the estimates obtained in the subsequent models could be biased because of the common method used. In order to test whether or not common method variance is a relevant issue in our study, we followed the confirmatory factor analysis approach suggested by Williams and McGonagle (2016). In particular, we first estimated a Baseline Model, in which all latent vari- ables were composed by their respective observed variables and co- varied. Then, we included in the model an unmeasured latent method construct (ULMC)—defined by Williams and McGonagle (2016) as a presumed source of common method variance that is not included in the data—that loaded on all observed variables and did not covary with substantive factors. In particular, we estimated three models: A model in which method factor loadings (MFLs) of ULMC are uncon- strained (Method Uu Model); an intermediate model, in which MFLs of ULMC of variables belonging to the different latent dimensions are separately (within factor) constrained to be equal (Method Ui Model); a model in which MFLs of ULMC are all constrained to be equal (Method Uc Model). The fit of each model was compared to the fit of Baseline Model: A significant difference would support the hypoth- esis that common method variance may represent a serious threat to data, because adding ULMC significantly improve the goodness of fit; on the contrary, a non-significant difference would attest that no relevant common method variance is present, because the inclu- sion of ULMC does not improve the goodness of fit. Results showed the following fit indices for Baseline Model: YBχ2(212) = 422.793, SCF = 1.1159, p < .001; CFI = .960; TLI = 0.948; RMSEA = 0.050; SRMR = 0.047. Then, Method Uu Model and Method Ui Model did not converge, whereas Method Uc Model showed the following fit indices: YBχ2(211) = 437.494, SCF = 1.0637, p < .001; CFI = .957; TLI = 0.944; RMSEA = 0.052; SRMR = 0.047. The scaled difference chi-square (ΔSBχ2), devised by Satorra and Bentler (2001), did not show significantly difference between Baseline Model and Method Uc Model (ΔSBχ2 = 0.530, Δdf = 1, p = .466). In conclusion, results would support the notion that common method variance is not a concern in our data.

text_extraction: To investigate the presence of common method variance (CMV) in our model we used the six-factor measurement model and the unmeasured latent method construct (ULMC) approach (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003). Because of identification prob- lems, we restricted all item loadings on the ULMC to be equal, the cor- relations between the ULMC and the other latent factors to be zero, and the variance of the ULMC to be 1. The significance of the factor loadings was examined both with and without the ULMC in the model in order to determine if the ULMC had an effect on the parameters (Podsakoff et al., 2003). There were minimal differences (<0.001) in the factor loadings between the model with the CMV factor and with- out it. In addition, the model fit did not improve significantly when adding the CMV factor (Δχ2 = 1.43, ΔCFI = 0.00, ΔRMSEA = 0.00). This shows that our model is at least not contaminated by an ULMC (Williams, Cote, & Buckley, 1989) and therefore we excluded it in our main analyses. However, the above does not rule out the presence of CMV as all available post hoc statistical remedies for its detection have been criticized (Richardson, Simmering, & Sturman, 2009). There- fore, it is relevant to consider the implications of its possible presence in this study, but it is not a major concern as we are mainly examining the relative importance and interaction effects of our two independent variables. We return to this issue in the Limitations section.

text_extraction: This study encountered several limitations that can be addressed in future research. First, this study employed a quantitative survey to examine the linkages between supervisors’ use of motivating language, employees’ psychological need satisfaction, and employee trust. To gain an in-depth understanding of how supervisory leadership communication influences employee trust during the pandemic, future studies can uti- lize qualitative approaches such as interviews, case studies, and focus groups. Future research can also focus on a single type of organization or a particular industry (e.g., healthcare, or other essential businesses), or a specific group of employees such as front-line workers during the pandemic to offer more context-specific insights regard- ing leadership communication during the pandemic. Additionally, the cross-sectional survey design with self-reported data may be subject to common method variance (CMV). Although the use of Harman’s single factor test and the unmeasured latent method factor technique (Fuller et al., 2016; Richardson et al., 2009) did not reveal common source bias in our data, we suggest future research adopt a mixed-method approach or include two or more information sources to rule out any potential CMV influence. Relatedly, although SEM analysis is an advantageous statistical tool in test- ing priori conceptual models derived from the literature (Kline, 2011), it is limited in establishing true causal relationships. Therefore, we suggest future researchers use experimental and longitudinal designs to further examine the order of effects in our model. Furthermore, this study focused on exploring employee psychological need for competence and relatedness, which are identified as salient mental and emotional needs of employees during the pandemic. Finally, this study focused on supervisory use of motivating language in the U.S. Since the COVID-19 pandemic is a global disease outbreak, it is worthy of examining how the effectiveness of leaders’ use of motivating language may be influenced by national culture and socioeconomic contexts.

However, given the large number of items (31 items) for this analysis compared to the low sample size (N = 138), we applied the item parcelling technique to the items of the trait mindfulness, the work engagement and the innovative work behaviour scales (Little et al., 2002). Specifically, following Little et al.’s (2002) recommendation, we first conducted a one‐factor CFA for each construct and then created three parallel parcels (indicators) per latent factor by combining items with higher factor loadings with those with lower factor loadings. The hypothesized five‐factor model displayed a good fit to the data (χ2 [94] = 134.50, CFI = 0.96, RMSEA = 0.06, SRMR = 0.06) and outperformed both a four‐factor model combining work engagement and intrinsic motivation (χ2 [98] = 219.25, CFI = 0.87, RMSEA = 0.09, SRMR = 0.07; Δχ2 [4] = 84.75, p < 0.01) and a one‐factor model (χ2 [104] = 606.58, CFI = 0.48, RMSEA = 0.19, SRMR = 0.13; Δχ2 [10] = 472.08, p < 0.01). However, because intrinsic motivation, work engagement and innovative work behaviour were measured at the same time by the same source, the hypothesized relationship between these variables could be inflated by common method variance. Accordingly, we used the unmeasured latent method factor technique (Podsakoff et al., 2012) to examine this issue within CFA. This approach is rec- ommended when the specific source of method bias is unknown or cannot be measured (Williams, Cote, & Buckley et al., 1989), as in the present study. The CFA model for intrinsic motivation and innovative work yielded a better fit to the data after the inclusion of the method factor (Δχ2 [9] = 21.13, p < 0.01). However, the method factor explained 24.17% of the total variance, which is not higher than the median amount of method variance (25%) observed in self‐report research (Podsakoff et al., 2012; Williams et al., 1989). Therefore, although common method bias cannot be fully ruled out, it is unlikely to invalidate our study's findings. text_extraction: To test for common method variance (CMV) and its poten- tial biasing effects in sample 1, we conducted CFAs using the unmeasured latent method factor approach (Williams & McGonagle, 2016). After evaluating a five-factor measure- ment model (with NWRR, time-based WLC, strain-based WLC, mindfulness, and psychological detachment) and establishing acceptable fit (CFI = 0.94, RMSEA = 0.07), we added an orthogonal latent common method factor (CMF) to the basic measurement model to test for presence and equal- ity of method effects. The CMF accounted for an average of 26.57% of the variance in the substantive indicators, which is just above the recommended median amount of method variance (25%; Williams et al., 1989) and well below the cut-off of 70% (Fuller et al., 2016). To test for CMV in sample 2, we followed two recom- mended approaches (Williams & McGonagle, 2016) to improve on the limitations of the unmeasured latent con- struct approach. The marker variable approach involves an indirect measure of the variable presumed to underlie the CMV. We selected community satisfaction as our marker variable as it may capture sources of CMV related to affect- driven response tendencies likely to impact NWRR measure- ment (and other substantive variables in the present study, e.g., WLC), but does not directly measure this response ten- dency. The measured cause variable approach helps detect direct sources of method effects by including the measure- ment of a method latent variable presumed to be a source of CMV (Simmering et al., 2015). Negative affect is a potential source of CMV that, if present, should be controlled for in the present study, as NWRR has an affective component and we assessed affect-based outcomes (e.g., emotional exhaus- tion, career satisfaction). We evaluated the full 12-factor measurement model (NWRR, five criterion-validity variables, and six dis- criminant validity variables) and established good fit (CFI = 0.902, RMSEA = 0.055). Then, we estimated two additional measurement models with the addition of the method variables. In the first model, we added community satisfaction as the marker variable, and in the second model we added negative affect as the measured cause variable. In each respective model, the method latent variable was linked to all of the study indicators, but was not allowed to correlate with the substantive latent variables. The marker method factor accounted for an average of 2.69% of the variance in the substantive indicators, and the measured cause factor accounted for an average of 9.47% of the variance in the substantive indicators, which are below the recommended cut-off (25%; Williams et al., 1989). These findings indicate CMV had little effect on our validity tests.

text_extraction: As employees were nested within groups, we conducted mul- tilevel confirmatory factor analyses (MCFAs). We were inter- ested in the constructs at the individual level and did not con- ceptualize the corresponding constructs at the group level. Therefore, the MCFA models did not assume the existence of group-level constructs but allowed for group-level variabil- ity on each item with a saturated model of the covariances among them (Kim et al., 2016; Stapleton et al., 2016). We conducted item-level MCFAs. The model fit of the hypothe- sized seven-factor model (χ2 = 461.29, df = 254, p < .01, CFI = .94, TLI = .85, RMSEA = .05, SRMRwithin = .05, SRMRbetween = .06) is shown in Table 1. The TLI value was lower than the recommended cutoff value of .90 (Bentler, 1989; Bentler & Bonett, 1980). Nonetheless, the cutoff crite- rion should not be strictly applied to MCFAs as it was pro- posed in the context of single-level CFAs (Dyer et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2016). We also used factor loadings and factor correlations to evaluate the hypothesized seven-factor model. The factor loadings ranged from .50 to .93 (all p-values < .001), surpassing the recommended cutoff value of .40 (Ferris et al., 2008; Hinkin, 1998). The correlational effect sizes between the factors ranged from .01 to .49, smaller than .50 (i.e., the recommended cutoff value for large correlational effect size; Cohen, 1988). These results suggested that all items adequately reflected the corresponding latent factors, and each latent factor was distinct. Thus, the hypothesized seven-factor model was acceptable. We then compared the hypothesized seven-factor model with three alternative models (alternative model 1, combining quantitative and qualitative job insecurity; alternative model 2, combining psychological safety and meaningfulness; alterna- tive model 3, combining APGO and LGO). Chi-square differ- ence tests showed that the hypothesized seven-factor model fitted the data significantly better than the three alternative models (alternative model 1, Δχ2(6) = 211.32, p < .01; alter- native model 2, Δχ2(6) = 329.79, p < .01; alternative model 3, Δχ2(6) = 452.98, p < .01), supporting the discriminant valid- ity of our measures. As all variables were reported by em- ployees, we conducted analyses to check for common method variance (Podsakoff et al., 2003; Podsakoff et al., 2012). Harman’s single-factor test revealed that seven factors emerged with eigenvalues greater than 1 and the largest factor explained only 21% of the variance, suggesting that common method variance was not a serious concern in our study (Podsakoff & Organ, 1986). We also used the unmeasured latent method factor technique to detect common method var- iance. Specifically, we added an uncorrelated method factor to the hypothesized seven-factor model and connected all items to the method factor. The average variance explained by the method factor was 9%, which is less than the 25% average in the literature (Neubert et al., 2016; Williams et al., 1989). Thus, our findings are unlikely to have been heavily influ- enced by common method variance.

text_extraction: For Study 1, given the cross-sectional design of our data sample, we used a single unmeasured latent method factor to minimize common method variance (CMV), according to the recommendations by Podsakoff et al. (2003). The CMV reflects the systematic variance among all items in the model other than the covariance among the constructs (Hulland, Baumgartner, and Smith 2018; Podsakoff et al. 2003). Our results for Study 1 showed that even after includ- ing the CMV in the confirmatory factorial analysis, the loadings to latent constructs of our model remained positive and significant for all items and was not significantly changed (loadings change an average of .06). This procedure agrees with suggestions from Malhotra, Kim, and Patil (2006). Moreover, the model fit indicators (e.g., CFI, AGFI, and RMSEA) also remained good and unchanged. These results indicated that the influence of CMV is minimal (Hulland, Baumgartner, and Smith 2018). For Study 2, using multisource data reduces risks con- nected with common source biases (Podsakoff et al. 2003). Thus, we used data from salespeople and their companies. Previous sales studies have used this method of employing multisource data (see Gabler et al. 2017). In addition, using a procedure like Bachrach, Mullins, and Rapp (2017), we condensed the use of extensive scales, because our sample refers to salespeople assessing the perceptions of their man- agers working with both controls. Third, we measured sales performance in terms of efficiency, as used by Schmitz, Lee, and Lilien (2014), mixing subjective and objective measures. Therefore, we considered all concerns suggested by Hulland, Baumgartner, and Smith (2018) for dealing with common method bias.

The analysis indicates that the common variance is less than 11 percent; further, the item loadings on the common method factor were not statistically significant and were much lower than the load- ings on their respective constructs. Comparing the model fit of these two different models, the model with and the model without common method factor also revealed that the inclusion of common method factor did not change the value of the model fit (CMIN/DF values were 1.29 and 1.28, respectively). Finally, a CFA model, which had a common latent factor, was used to impute the factor scores for the creation of the interaction terms in the model. We added a common latent factor to the full structural model and associated it with the indicators of the constructs. This enabled us to partial out any possible effect of common method bias on the structural model. The results indicate that after including a common latent factor in the full structural model, the estimates for the hypothesized effects remained virtually the same, which also suggests that common method bias did not affect the results. In sum, the results of the above analyses provide confidence that CMB is not a concern in this study.

text_extraction: We examined the robustness of the results with four approaches. First, as Podsakoff et al. (2003) recommend, we employed Harman’s one- factor test. This test assesses the threat of common method bias by indicating whether a single latent factor offers a viable alternative explanation of the analysis. The one-factor latent model yielded a chi-square of 6063.27 (d.f. = 209). The fit of the one-factor model was significantly worse than that of the measurement model. Therefore, we gained preliminary evidence that the measurement model was robust to common method variance. Second, considering possible limitations of Harman’s one-factor test, we employed Lindell and Whitney’s (2001) marker variable assessment technique. We chose attractiveness of uploaded photos (AUP) as the marker variable for the analysis, because it is theoretically unrelated to our dependent variable of we-intentions. The we-intentions and AUP exhibited nonsignificant correlations of .02. Therefore, we used AUP’s measured correlation with the dependent variable as an indication of method variance. None of the significant correlations in the overall model became insignificant after adjustment, providing additional evidence against the existence of common method bias in our data. Third, we added an unmeasured latent method factor and allowed all self-reported items to load on both their theoretical constructs and the method factor (Bagozzi 2011). This model fit well: χ2[199] = 451.31, p . .00, RMSEA = .036, SRMR = .035, NNFI = .99, and CFI = .99. All item loadings on the common method factor were much lower than the loadings on their respective constructs, and the structural model estimates for our hypothesized effects remained virtually unchanged after we introduced the method factor, which also suggests that common method bias did not bias the results. Finally, common method bias was unlikely to explain the hypothesized moderating effect of members’ experience level on the link between we-intentions and contribution behavior, because the survey respondents should not have easily anticipated any complicated interactive relationships in the framework (Aiken and West 1991). Collectively, across the four criteria we examined, we can conclude that common method bias does not present a significant threat to the study.

text_extraction: To control the results for potential common-method bias, a single unmeasured latent method factor was intro- duced in the causal model. That is, an unmeasured latent construct was added, and all items were allowed to load on their theoretical constructs, as well as on the latent common-methods variance factor. This procedure allows controlling the portion of variance in the indicators due to their same source and other same-method effects. For identification purposes, method factor loadings had to be constrained to be equal when estimating this model (Podsakoff et al., 2003). Examination of the significance of the structural parameters with and without this factor in the model showed a similar fit of the model when the common-methods variance factor was included. Besides the previously encountered significant positive effect of perceived advantages on behavioral intention formulated in H2, which turned out to become nonsignificant, all other path effects remained the same (i.e., the effects that were significant or nonsignificant when common-method vari- ance was not controlled remained significant or nonsig- nificant when it was controlled) (Podsakoff et al., 2003). While these relationships were not strongly affected by the common-method variance factor, they changed slightly. The relationship between perceived advantages and atti- tude as well as subjective norms and behavioral intention decreased to a small extent, while the relationship between perceived behavioral control and the relationship some- what increased (Table 7). Overall, common-method bias slightly affected but did not change the picture of the presented results. In line with Spector (2006), the study has established that the variables of interest are related. Future research may “do a series of studies and analyses to control and test for plausible biases that might have dis- torted the observed relationship” (Spector, 2006, p. 230).

text_extraction: One important issue with all self-report data is the common method variance (CMV) (Podsakoff & Organ, 1986). Therefore, we informed all the respondents that their responses would be confidential and for academic research purposes only to reduce common method bias (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003). In addition, we first conducted a Harmon’s single factor test to check it. We performed an exploring factor analysis on all independent and dependent variables. The results show that the top nine factors (we measured a total of nine independent and dependent variables through the question- naire) can explain 71.94 percent of total variance, which is more than 60 percent, and there is no one fac- tor which can explain more than 30 percent of the total variance. In addition, we used the most rigorous tests based on confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to assess and control for CMV (Podsakoff et al., 2003). We added an unmeasured latent method factor in the CFA model, making each item an indicator of both its substantive trait and the latent method factor. Then, we compared the new model fit indices and factor loading of each indicator with the basic model to ver- ify the extent of changes to the model fit. Our results show that the model fit indices become limited bet- ter with the latent method factor (e.g., as for subjective value of negotiation outcome, v2/df is decreased from 1.95 to 1.78 (change of 8%); GFI is increased from 0.90 to 0.91 (change of 0.8%); CFI is increased from 0.95 to 0.96 (change of 0.9%); IFI is increased from 0.95 to 0.96 (change of 0.9%). As for negotia- tion behavior, v2/df is decreased from 1.84 to 1.64 (change of 11%); GFI is increased from 0.87 to 0.88 (change of 1.4%); CFI is increased from 0.91 to 0.93 (change of 2.5%); IFI is increased from 0.91 to 0.93 (change of 2.4%). All the model fit indices’ changes are lower than the average level of 25 percent observed by Williams, Cote, and Buckley (1989), and 16 percent observed by Carlson and Perrewe (1999) which indicates that our research did not suffer from a serious disturbance of CMV.

text_extraction: he existence of common method bias (CMV) can be fatal, particularly in mediation studies where the data are collected through self-report questionnaires. Therefore, we used proactive measures to prevent these biases, and then ex-post statistical techniques (Podsakoff et al. 2003), to weigh to what extent our results are affected by common method biases (see also, Conway and Lance 2010). In the proactive case, our surveyors guaranteed respondents’ confidentiality and anonymity in order to diminish the social desirability bias. In addition, the researchers separated the items of anomia from those of employees’ perceived interpersonal deviance, and these two scales’ items appeared on different pages of the questionnaire. This yielded an effect of psy- chological separation in the respondents (Podsakoff et al. 2003). In the ex-post statistical technique, the possibility of common method bias (CMV) was tested using Harman’s one-factor test (Podsakoff and Organ 1986). Following Harman’s one-factor test, we used exploratory factor anal- ysis (EFA) for item reduction, but fixing only one factor to extract and with no rotation. The principal component factor analysis conducted on the items of anomia and interpersonal deviance, and the factors of uncompassionate feeling, yiel- ded a unique factor that explains 14.39 % of the variance (rule of thumb establishes that if the factor explains more than 25 %, it suggests significant CMV). In addition, we employed CFA to test the fit of a one-factor model (where negative judgments about others, over-identification, isola- tion, and interpersonal deviance items were loaded in a single factor) and the five-factor model. The results showed that the fit of the five-factor solution (v2 = 344.202, df = 142, p\.001; CFI = .89; IFI = .89; TLI = .86; NFI = .83; RMSEA = .061) is significantly better (Dv d2 (10) = 904.174, p \ .001) than the one-factor model (v2 = 1248.376, df = 152, p \ .001; CFI = .41; IFI = .42; NFI = .39; TLI = .26; RMSEA = .161), supporting no significant CMV. The final statistical procedure to check for CMV involved controlling for the effects of an unmeasured latent method construct by specifying a latent CMV factor on which all the manifest indicators load. All the regression weights have to be constrained to be equal. The fit indices of this model with the CMV factor (v2 = 319.324, df = 141, p \ .001; CFI = .860; IFI = .859; TLI = .810; NFI = .801; RMSEA = .067) was worse than the fit of the CFA model without the CMV factor (v2 = 344.202, df = 142, p\.001; CFI = .89; IFI = .89; TLI = .86; NFI = .83; RMSEA = .061), as the Chi square difference test was significant (Dv d2(1) = 24.878, p \ .001). More- over, each of the regression weights was .28, which squared results in about 7.84 % of common variance. All of the above patterns suggest that CMV exists, but it was not a major problem for the data (Podsakoff et al. 2003).

Podsakoff et al., 2003). Although CMB cannot inflate (but does deflate) interaction effect (P. M. Podsakoff et al., 2012), which is the central issue of this research, we evaluated whether CMB might be a threat to the underlying data. We employed two statistical post hoc techniques to assess whether variance in our data could be attrib- uted to a single factor. First, we conducted a confirmatory factor analysis to test model fit difference between the one-factor model and a multifactor model (Craighead et al., 2011). The one-factor model (χ2 = 5,829.22, df = 702, p < .001) fit significantly worse than the multifactor model (χ2 = 1,182.58, df = 692, p < .001), implying that CMB does not pose a serious threat (Δχ2 =4,646.64, Δdf = 10, p < .001). Second, we ran a confirmatory factor analysis controlling for the effects of a single unmeasured latent method factor (P. M. Podsakoff et al., 2003), allowing all indicators in the mea- surement model to load on an unmeasured method factor as well as their respective factors. The common latent factor accounted for 12% of the total variance, which is well below the 25% threshold (Williams et al., 1989). Thus, CMB is not a problem in the present case.

text_extraction: Lastly, given that the variables in our study were collected at the same time and obtained by the same method (self-report questionnaires), com- mon method variance might have affected the strength of observed rela- tionships. Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, and Podsakoff (2012) recommend a series of methods to evaluate the potential effect of common method var- iance. In the current study, we adopted the technique of controlling for the effects of a single unmeasured latent method factor. Utilising this method we found that common method variance was not a factor that affected the strength of the relationships in our study. Specifically, we used the unmeasured latent method factor (UMLMF) technique (Podsak- off, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003) to detect common variance shared among substantive indicators that are not due to random error or the substantive constructs. Using Amos 19 (Arbuckle, 2010), we added a common latent factor to a measurement model that included all the studys variables. We then added regression lines from the common factor to every observed item in the model. This way we could determine the amount of variance that is commonly shared among all the observed items in the model. We found that the proportion of variance attributed to method is 17 per cent. Given that this is lower than the 25 per cent threshold, we conclude that the common method variance present in our data is not sufficient to bias results (e.g. see Choi & Chen, 2007).

text_extraction: To address the common methods variance issue empirically, we used Harman's one-factor test and the unmeasured latent method factor technique. First, individual unit members' responses (n = 701) to the items that were used to create this study's support climate (five items), affective commitment (eight items), in-role behavior (seven items), OCBI (seven items), and OCBO (seven items) variables were entered in a principal components extraction factor analysis, and the results of the unrotated solution were examined (see Way et al., 2010). Six factors with an eigenvalue greater than 1 emerged from this analysis, and no single factor accounted for most of the variance. Thus, the results of Harman's one-factor test indicate that common method variance is not a problem in this current study (see Podsak- off & Organ, 1986; Way et al., 2010). Next, we used the unmeasured latent method factor technique, which involves adding a first-order method factor whose only mea- sures are the indicators of the measurement model's factors that share a common method (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, & Podsakoff, 2012). The CFA of the five-factor (support climate, affective commitment, in-role behavior, OCBI, and OCBO) measurement model in which all items were specified to load onto their respective five factors demon- strated a good fit with the data (n = 682): χ2517 = 1385.07, p < .001; RMSEA = 0.05; standardized root mean square residual (SRMR) = 0.04; CFI = 0.93; TLI = 0.93.3 Similarly, the CFA of the six- factor measurement model in which an unmeasured latent methods factor was added to the five-factor measurement model and all items were specified to load onto their respective five factors as well as the unmeasured latent methods factor demonstrated a good fit with the data (n = 682): χ2490 = 1322.76, p < .001; RMSEA = 0.05; SRMR = 0.07; CFI = 0.93; TLI = 0.92. The comparison of the goodness-of-fit of these models was calculated by CFI difference. The change of CFI between the five-factor measurement model and the six-factor mea- surement model (0.003) is well below the suggested rule of thumb of 0.05 (Bagozzi & Yi, 1990). Thus, one can conclude that including the unmeasured latent methods factor in the measurement model does not significantly improve the overall fit of the measurement model. Together, these results indicate that common method variance is not a problem in this current study.

text_extraction: Although they are regularly used in business re- search, self-reported measures with a common scale format and the potential to invoke social desirability are generally susceptible to common method bias. To reduce this effect, we ensured the respondents’ anonymity and common understanding of terms and explained the importance of providing motivated and conscientious answers (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, & Podsakoff, 2012). We performed several statistical pro- cedures to detect potential common method bias. First, we conducted Harman’s single-factor test, loading 14 self-reported variables on one factor and using an exploratory principal axis factoring without rotation. One factor explained only 29.9% of variance; hence, it did not indicate a potential common method bias (Podsakoff et al., 2003). Next, we ran a single-factor model based on confirmatory factor analysis. The model had an unacceptable fit (x2 5 291.89, df 5 35.16, p , .05, RMSEA 5 .13, SRMR 5 .12, NNFI 5 .71). Last, we tested a measurement model with the addition of a single, unmeasured latent method factor using all ob- served variables as its indicators (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003; Podsakoff et al., 2012). This model yielded an improper solution, indicating a po- tentially serious misfit. Although no statistical test can completely exclude the possibility of common method bias, the results provide evidence that it most likely does not threaten the validity of our results.

text_extraction: Common method variance (CMV) can be a significant source of measurement error (Pod- sakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, and Podsakoff, 2003). To help reduce CMV, best practices were used, including (1) assuring respondent anonymity, (2) informing the respondent that there were no correct or incorrect answers to prevent evaluation apprehension (Podsakoff et al., 2003), and (3) varying scale anchors (Rind- fleisch, Malter, Ganesan, and Moorman, 2008). CMV was assessed through the CFA version of Harman’s single-factor test. The measurement model was com- pared with an alternative model in which all items load on a single, common construct. Should the alter- native model explain a majority of the covariance, as evidenced by a nonsignificant chi-square change between the measurement model and CMV model, CMV is likely to be an issue (Podsakoff et al., 2003). The results show that CMV is unlikely to be a con- cern, as the chi-square change between models is large (v2(21) 5 3,812.65) and significant (p < .0001). In addition, to further account for CMV, the unmeasured latent method factor technique was used (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, and Podsakoff, 2012). A com- mon method factor in the CFA model was included, with all items loading on their proposed constructs as well as the common method factor. This approach extracts the CMV and accounts for systemic biases (Podsakoff et al., 2012). Subsequent to the inclusion of the common method factor, latent variable scores were estimated and then used them to test the path model. Model estimation and accounting for direct effects of antecedent variables. The latent variable scores approach was used to test the hypothesized relation- ships (J€oreskog and Yang, 2000). Latent variable scores (factor scores) were extracted from the CFA model that included the unmeasured latent method. actor to account for CMV.

text_extraction: Given that our variables were measured based on self-reported experiences, we tested the presence and magnitude of common method variance in our data using a single unmeasured latent method factor technique recommended by Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, and Podsakoff (2003). By using Mplus version 8.0 (Muthén & Muthén, 1998-2018), we compared three models, a nine-factor measurement model, a measurement model with an orthogonal method factor, and a revised method factor model by constraining correlations among the nine factors to the correlation obtained from the nine-factor only model. We used chi-square tests, comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker- Lewis Index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean-square residual (SRMR) to evaluate measurement models (Hu & Bentler, 1999). The nine-factor and an orthogonal method factor model, χ2(627) = 1415.457, p < .001, CFI = .889, TLI = .869, RMSEA = .073, 95% CI [0.068, 0.079], SRMR = .056, fitted better than the nine-factor only model, χ2(666) = 2055.093, p < .001, CFI = .805, TLI = .783, RMSEA = .095, 95% CI [0.090, 0.099], SRMR = .099; particularly, variance partitioning showed that 19.40% of variance was attributed to the method factor, which is smaller than a median amount of variance 25% from other self-reported studies (Williams, Cote, & Buckley, 1989). Additionally, the fit of a revised model, χ2(663) = 1457.204, p < .001, CFI = .889, TLI = .875, RMSEA = .072, 95% CI [0.067, 0.077], SRMR = .076, did not change significantly (Δχ2 = 41.747, Δdf = 36, p = .235), which showed little evidence for common method variance. text_extraction: Following best practices for handling common method variance (CMV) in IB research (Chang, van Witteloostuijn, & Eden, 2010), we employed several strategies to avoid CMV ex ante and to control for it ex post: (1) To avoid any potential CMV in the research design stage, we used information from different sources for our key measures with a time lag. In particular, we divided the questionnaire into three parts and had more than one person answer the questionnaire as much as possible, we collected data on the dependent variables (e.g., firm perfor- mance) for an interval of several months, and we incorporated data from multiple sources (e.g., survey and archival data) into the estimation model. (2) We designed complicated specifications of regression models with the aim of creating cognitive difficulties for respondents to infer the exact goal of the research. Specifically, we included two interactions in our model, which makes CMV less likely to affect our estimation. (3) Researchers frequently use a post hoc Harman one-factor analysis to check whether variation in the data can be largely attributed to a single factor. We conducted a principal components factor test of all questionnaire-based variables. The test did not yield one overarching factor, which suggested the absence of CMV. (4) To further ensure that CMV bias was not a serious concern, we added a first-order factor (a single unmeasured latent method factor) to the hypothesized measurement model (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003). The increase in model fit obtained by accounting for the common method factor was not significant, and the variance extracted by the method factor was only 0.16, which was well below the 0.50 cutoff. (5) Finally, we conducted a marker variable test (Lindell & Whitney, 2001). We used a dummy variable that was theoretically unrelated to our principal con- structs: whether the number of strokes of the com- pany name in Chinese was even. The results showed that the average correlation between our principal constructs and the marker variable was.08 (p > 0.10). These efforts confirmed that the CMV bias was insignificant in this study.

text_extraction: We applied statistical remedies to account for common method biases (Podsakoff et al. 2012) that may undermine the empirical validity of results. Three a priori models of the variables included in our hypotheses were compared: a one-factor model, in which all items loaded on a common factor, was tested against a full measurement four-factor model, in which the items loaded on their respective factor (i.e., authentic leadership, leader work–life balance, fol- lower work–life balance, job satisfaction), and a five-factor model, in which all items were further constrained to load equally on an unmeasured latent method factor. For each model, we report the v2 value, degrees of freedom, and probability value, as well as one index to describe incre- mental fit (i.e., the comparative fit index, CFI) and one residual-based fit index (i.e., the root mean square error of approximation, RMSEA), and the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR). Approximate fit indices are used for evaluative model comparisons as indicated in the lit- erature (Goffin 2007). The following standards were applied: CFI greater than .90, RMSEA equal to or lower than .06, SRMR equal to or lower than .08 (Nye and Drasgow 2011; Hu and Bentler 1998, 1999), and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) with lower values indicating better fit (Preacher and Merkle 2012). CFA with maximum likelihood estimation yielded the following results. Comparing the one-factor model (v2(299, 121) = 1031.717, p \ .001, RMSEA = .142, SRMR = .108, CFI = .650, BIC = 8656.249) to the four-factor model (v2 (293, 121) = 534.490, p \ .001, RMSEA = .083, SRMR = .066, CFI = .885, BIC = 8187.796), indicators point to the fact that overall the four-factor model fits the data better (v2diff = 497.23, p \ .001). Comparing the four-factor model and the five-factor model with an unmeasured latent method factor (v2(288, 121) = 475.396, p \ .001, RMSEA = .073, SRMR = .073, CFI = .910, BIC = 8152.682), the five-factor model showed a better fit (v2diff = 59.093, p \ .001). Overall, we acknowledge that an unmeasured latent method factor influenced our data. However, the theoretically derived four- factor model was only slightly inferior to the five-factor model, and was clearly better suited to fit the data than a one- factor model, which did not differentiate between the vari- ables of interest. Based on the empirical evidence and our theoretical reasoning, we conclude that data related to the four factors provide meaningful information.

text_extraction: n addition, we used Harman’s one-factor test to check for common method variance (CMV), which may be caused by self-report single source data. If CMV is a serious problem, a single factor should emerge from a factor analysis (Scott & Bruce, 1994). This means that if the one-factor model fits the data well in CFA, we would expect a severe impact of CMV on our results (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003). The CFA results (see Table 1) showed that the one-fac- tor model did not fit the data adequately (χ2[df = 119] = 1137.10, χ2/df = 9.56, SRMR = .16, RMSEA = .18, CFI = .57), suggesting that CMV might not be a signif- icant issue in our study. To further reduce this concern, we followed past research (e.g. Castanheira, 2015; Podsakoff et al., 2003) to conduct a more rigorous test. Specifically, we tested a three-factor model with the addition of an unmeasured latent method factor. In this method model, all items loaded on their correspond- ing constructs as well as on this method factor. Results (see Table 1) demon- strated a good fit for this model (χ2[df = 99] = 201.15, χ2/df = 2.03, SRMR = .04, RMSEA = .06, CFI = .96). Despite the identical observed items for both models, the three-factor model cannot be nested within the model with a method factor (Castanheira, 2015), thus the change in CFI was used for comparison. Since the CFI change was .03, which is smaller than the rule of thumb of .05 proposed by Bagozzi and Yi (1990), the influence of the method factor could be regarded as not significant. In addition, although the method factor slightly increased the model fit, the explanatory power of this factor accounted for only 22.94% of the method variance, which is less than 25–40% that prior scholars suggested and observed to be reasonable (Williams, Cote, & Buckley, 1989). These analyses indicated that CMV was less likely to severely distort our results.

text_extraction: Fifth and finally, we used the unmeasured latent method construct (ULMC) approach as recommended by Podsakoff et al. (2003) to detect CMV. In this approach, the ULMC only loads on all items of the latent variables (Podsakoff et al., 2003). Adding the ULMC enhanced the fit of the model (see Table 2). This enhancement can be explained by the fact that this model has more parameters and fewer degrees of freedom (Ng & Feldman, 2013). According to Brammer, He, and Mellahi (2015), CMV can be excluded when the items of corresponding variables load higher than.50 and the loadings on the ULMC either should be smaller than those on the latent variables or non-significant. Table 2 shows that the standardized factor loadings of our constructs are all signifi- cant and all above.50 except for ABS3 (.47). All standardized factor loadings of the ULMC are considerably below the threshold of.50 (Hair et al., 2010). Again, the exception is the standardized factor loading ABS3 on the ULMC (.63). Moreover, only one factor loading of the ULMC is significant (ABS3) and 14 are non-signifi- cant. This suggests CMV to be present. The threshold of.50 (Hair et al., 2010) was not exceeded regarding the AVE of the ULMC (AVE =.0490) and 4.90 % of the variance was accounted for by CMV. Concern about inflated relationships would come up if CMV would reach a percentage of 70 % (Fuller, Simmering, Atinc, At- inc, & Babin, 2016). From the ULMC approach, it can be concluded that CMV is present, however it does not pose a serious threat to the data in the present study (Conway & Lance, 2010; Podsakoff et al., 2003).

text_extraction: ne of the most critical problems in survey‐based research which mea- sures dependent and independent variables from the same source is certainly common method variance. It is defined as variance that is attributable to the measurement method rather than to the construct of interest (Campbell & Fiske, 1959). Therefore, it could produce biased results. Since we used self‐reported data and all variables are measured using the same source, we need to control for the presence of common method variance and whether it has generated any sys- tematic error. Among business researchers, there is an ongoing debate on the problems deriving from common method variance (Richardson, Simmering, & Sturman, 2009). For instance, a recent work from Fuller, Simmering, Atinc, Atinc, and Babin (2016) has empirically demon- strated that common method variance is able to produce a systematic, and negative, effect only when it is present at relatively high levels, and these cases are not very common in practice. However, we tested for the presence of common method variance by performing two statistical techniques. First of all, we checked whether common method variance affects our data by performing the controversial Harman's single‐factor post‐hoc test (Podsakoff & Organ, 1986). Even if the reliability of this test was considered questionable (Podsakoff et al., 2003), Fuller et al. (2016) have shown that these criti- cisms are partially unfounded. Moreover, they found that false‐negative cases (when the Harman test indicates that a common method variance is not present even if it occurs) are less common than false positives. The false‐positive cases may occur in high‐reliability datasets when Cronbach's alpha is higher than 0.95 (which is not the case in this study). The Harman test showed that the largest distinct factor accounted for 31% of the variance and seven factors with an eigenvalue greater than 1.0 emerged. Therefore, since no single factor emerged which accounts for the majority of covariance among the variables (Steensma, Tihanyi, Lyles, & Dhanaraj, 2005), it is possible to affirm that common method variance was not a concern. Moreover, we further tested for the presence of common method variance by performing the unmeasured latent method factor. This method was largely used in previous studies since it does not require the measurement of a specific factor which is responsible for the method variance (Podsakoff et al., 2003). According to the procedure described by Richardson et al. (2009), we estimated two measurement models. The first model includes the explored constructs with their manifest indicators (trait model). The second model comprises only the method constructs with paths to all manifest indicators (method model). Moreover, since the number of indicators of the constructs is not small relative to the number of constructs, a problem of under‐identi- fication should not occur. This test assumes that if the measurement model yields a better fit than the measurement model with a common factor, the findings are not biased. Table 2 shows the comparison among the models, based on a set of indicators and the chi‐square dif- ference test (Bentler & Bonnett, 1980), and demonstrates that the common factor model has a worse performance regarding data fit.
